origin: The four questions about a company's own documents come from Polaris Collective's working paper on model spec governance. The best practices beside them come from Kembery et al., Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs. Every row says which. Every score is ours, given by hand from public documents, and open to challenge.

memo.title: Model spec governance and transparency: the state of play and four transparency asks
memo.purpose: It sets out how companies govern their constitutions today and asks them for four kinds of transparency.

kembery.title: Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
kembery.purpose: It gathers the practices emerging internationally for writing, testing and governing a constitution.

columns.name: What is published
columns.plain: The rules anyone can read: whether a constitution exists and which models it covers, whether every change to the rules can be seen, which filters run around the models, what the model must never do, and whether the published text may be reused. It is half of the final score.
columns.about: This column is the part of governance a reader can check without being let in. Every row is a document, or something a document says: it exists or it does not, it names the models it governs or it does not, it records its changes or it does not. Eleven rows carry it, the ten checks of the four asks and the licence on the published text. Every row counts the same, so a question with three checks counts for three elevenths of the figure and one with two for two elevenths.

columns.name: What it engages
columns.plain: Whether the document binds the models: published tests of adherence, outside evaluators, a threshold a model must meet before release, who may approve a change, training on the document, the models the company uses internally, whether the published text is the one used inside, and monitoring in use. It is the other half of the final score.
columns.about: Nobody outside a company can watch it train, test or monitor a model, so no row here can be checked the way a published document can. What is scored is what each company publishes about its own practice, and a row scores 0 when we looked and found nothing. Eight rows carry it and each counts the same, so a group counts for as many eighths as it has practices. It is added to what is published to give the final score.

groups.name: Testing adherence
groups.plain: Whether anyone can see how well the models follow the constitution: a published test of adherence, outside evaluators with access to test it, and a threshold a model must meet before it is released.

groups.name: Change control
groups.plain: Who may change the constitution: whether the company publishes who approves a change, and whether a second team can veto one on safety grounds. Only the first is scored.

groups.name: Training and use
groups.plain: Whether the constitution is the text the models are actually held to: trained on, followed by the models the company uses internally, the same text inside as outside, and checked in use.

mark.drawn_as: the mark of X, the sign the company puts on itself

questions.name: Published constitution
questions.question: Does every model the company puts in use have a published constitution?
questions.plain: Whether the company publishes a constitution at all, and whether that document says which of its models it governs.
questions.explainer: A constitution is the document in which a company sets out how its models are meant to behave.

checks.label: A public constitution says how the model should behave in ordinary use

anchors.0: Nothing, or only a policy on how users may behave.
anchors.2: Partial: only prohibitions, with no description of good behaviour and no order of authority.
anchors.4: A full constitution: how the model should behave, how conflicts between instructions are settled, and who may instruct it at what level.

checks.reading: A 4 needs a document that says how the model should behave, and how a conflict between instructions is settled, as well as what it must refuse. The paper describes Google's policy guidelines for the Gemini app as prohibitions only, which is what a 2 describes.

quotes.text: checkable rules rather than long narrative, with default behaviour where no explicit rule applies and guidance for when principles conflict.
behaviour the developer has decided the model should exhibit and actively trains or enforces towards, whether or not current models exhibit it reliably.

quotes.where: Current status of model specs, on Google
quotes.text: This document only includes prohibitions, and does not include statements regarding positive behaviour, ordering of instructions, or anything on honesty.

checks.label: It says which models it covers, and the most-used ones are included

anchors.0: No statement of coverage, or the flagship models are left out.
anchors.2: Coverage is implied but not stated.
anchors.4: Coverage is stated, and the most-used models are in it.

checks.reading: A document that names no model cannot be tied to any product. A 4 needs the document to say which models it governs, and the most-used models to be among them. The memo states the principle; Kembery et al. spell out that the document itself should say which models it covers.

quotes.text: one spec may govern many models, but no deployed model goes ungoverned.

The spec should state which models it applies to. If a developer maintains multiple model families, fine-tuned variants, or specialised models (e.g. for internal deployment, code generation, or military applications), the spec should say which are covered.

quotes.where: Comparative assessment, scope carve-outs for Alibaba
quotes.text: The document names no model or deployment class it governs.

checks.label: Government, defence and other special deployments are covered, or the differences disclosed

anchors.0: Government, defence, specialised and large-scale internal deployments are not addressed.
anchors.2: The gap is acknowledged, but what applies instead is not disclosed.
anchors.4: They are covered, or the differences are published by kind of deployment.

checks.reading: The paper lets a company keep the rules of a government, defence or other special deployment private, provided their existence and their differences from the public document are published. A 4 is either full coverage or that disclosure. A company that says such deployments exist without saying what applies to them scores 2.

quotes.text: one spec may govern many models, but no deployed model goes ungoverned. That includes government, military and intelligence deployments, and models used internally at scale.

public in summary rather than in full. A published spec is the complete text, public. A disclosed spec is one whose existence, coverage and deviations from the public spec are public, while the content of specific rules may be redacted. For each deployment class the document covers, the lab publishes: which parts of the public spec carry over; where it deviates, by category; and for each hard constraint, whether it has been kept, changed or dropped. Three things are always public: that the document exists, which deployment classes it covers, and a dated log entry when it changes. Redaction can hide the content of the rules, never their existence, and that floor is what makes coverage of government and enterprise deployments workable.
one public spec plus a short statement per deployment class saying where it differs.

questions.reading: The question asks whether a company has written down, in public, how its models are meant to behave, and whether that document reaches every model it puts in use. The paper counts a model as in use when people outside the company use it, or when the company itself uses it at scale. The checks follow the paper's own parts: what makes a document a constitution, which models it covers, and the government, military and internal deployments the paper names.

quotes.text: Every model you deploy (internally at scale or externally) has a published governing spec.
one spec may govern many models, but no deployed model goes ungoverned. That includes government, military and intelligence deployments, and models used internally at scale.

quotes.where: Ask 1, what makes it a spec
quotes.text: all intended model behaviour is consistent with it, and no intended behaviour should be surprising in light of it. A deployment behaving under different rules with no governing document fails this test.

made available for use outside the lab (consumers, enterprises, or governments), or used inside the lab at scale, meaning sustained use in production workflows rather than research and testing. A model only touched in experiments is not deployed.

Two things: every deployed model has a governing spec (ask 1), and one change log with its scope and timeline stated up front (ask 2). The spec is the object; the log is the commitment. For labs that already publish a spec, ask 1 is mostly done and the log is the new work. Asks 3 and 4 are the direction of travel.

questions.name: Change log
questions.question: Is there one public change log covering the constitution, the system prompts and the guardrails?
questions.plain: Whether a reader can see what changed in the rules a model follows, when it changed and why.
questions.explainer: A system prompt is the standing instruction a company gives its model before every conversation.

checks.label: Every version is dated and kept online

anchors.0: No version number and no archive.
anchors.2: Versioned, but the archive is incomplete or not linked.
anchors.4: Every version is dated and can be retrieved at a permanent address.

checks.reading: The memo's ask takes versions for granted. The requirement that every version is dated and stays retrievable comes from Kembery et al., and it is here because a log of changes cannot be checked against versions nobody can find.

quotes.text: Updates require clear version control: a versioned, dated source document; a changelog recording changes and their reasoning, including when constraints are weakened or removed (e.g. OpenAI, 2025); publicly accessible prior versions;
a single public page listing every change, dated, with the diff and the reason.

checks.label: Each change is shown, with the reason for it

anchors.2: Summaries of what changed, without the changed text and without reasons.
anchors.4: The changed text, line by line, with the reason for each change.

checks.reading: A 4 needs, for every change, the changed text itself and the reason for it. A summary of what moved, without the text or the reason, is a 2.

quotes.text: a single public page listing every change, dated, with the diff and the reason.
The rationale costs nothing new; every change already has one in its internal review.

checks.label: The log also covers system prompts and guardrails, says which version of the constitution governs which model, and commits to a timeline

anchors.4: All three: the log spans system prompts and guardrails, says which version of the constitution governs which model, and commits to a period within which changes are logged.

checks.reading: Three things from the ask are counted together: the log covers system prompts and guardrails as well as the constitution, it says which version governs which model, and it commits to logging every change within a fixed number of days. One of the three is a 2, all three a 4.

quotes.text: the log opens with a one-paragraph scope statement (which layers and which deployments it covers) and a timeline: every change is entered within a fixed number of days of taking effect. That covers urgent changes too; a safeguard tightened overnight is logged inside the same window as everything else.
Each deployed model states which spec version governs it, so anyone can connect the rules to the model they are actually using.
behaviour can change in any layer, and today an outsider watching a model change cannot tell which layer moved.

questions.reading: The question asks for one public log in which every change to the rules a model follows can be found, whichever layer it happened in: the constitution, the system prompts or the guardrails. The checks separate keeping the versions, explaining each change, and the reach of the log.

quotes.text: Run one change log across spec, system prompts and guardrails: every spec change goes in, with diffs, reasons, a model-to-spec-version mapping, and a stated scope and timeline.

the log opens with a one-paragraph scope statement (which layers and which deployments it covers) and a timeline: every change is entered within a fixed number of days of taking effect. That covers urgent changes too; a safeguard tightened overnight is logged inside the same window as everything else. Changes to disclosed specs enter the same log, at deviation level: which deployment class, what date, and which category of deviation was added, changed, or removed.

Each deployed model states which spec version governs it, so anyone can connect the rules to the model they are actually using. Without the mapping, a reader can see the spec versions but cannot tell which one applied to the model in front of them.
a single public page listing every change, dated, with the diff and the reason.

Two things: every deployed model has a governing spec (ask 1), and one change log with its scope and timeline stated up front (ask 2). The spec is the object; the log is the commitment. For labs that already publish a spec, ask 1 is mostly done and the log is the new work. Asks 3 and 4 are the direction of travel.

questions.name: Guardrails
questions.question: Does the company disclose which guardrails it runs, and of what kind?
questions.plain: Whether the company says which automatic filters it runs around its models, and whether changes to them are recorded.
questions.explainer: Guardrails are automated checks, separate from the model itself, that block or redirect what goes in or comes out.

checks.label: The guardrails in use are disclosed, by kind

anchors.0: Nothing beyond general language about safety.
anchors.2: Disclosed for one product only, or as marketing.
anchors.4: A list by kind, across every product in use.

checks.reading: A 4 is an inventory of guardrails by kind that covers every product in use. Guardrails described for one product only, or in marketing, are a 2.

quotes.text: an initial inventory of guardrails by category, then log entries on change. The inventory is the real work; labs with safeguard reports have most of it written.

thresholds, prompts and detection logic stay undisclosed, and existence-and-category is information labs already publish piecemeal in system cards and safeguard reports; the ask only makes it systematic and dated.

checks.label: Changes to the guardrails are logged or announced systematically

anchors.0: Changes come to light through the press or through incidents.
anchors.2: Some are announced, but there is no register.
anchors.4: Every change is dated in the log.

checks.reading: A 4 is every change to a guardrail dated in the log. Changes that come to light only through the press or an incident are a 0.

quotes.text: System cards report how well a filter performs; they do not say when one was added, loosened, or removed, which is what the log adds.
Yet today a safeguard can be loosened or removed with nothing public to judge.
That covers urgent changes too; a safeguard tightened overnight is logged inside the same window as everything else.

questions.reading: The question asks for the list of filters a company runs around its models, by kind, with every change to them recorded. It asks for nothing that would help anyone get round them: thresholds, prompts and detection logic stay private.

quotes.text: Disclose guardrails: existence and category, changes in the log.

this follows from ask 1. If no intended behaviour should be surprising in light of the spec, behaviour enforced through classifiers cannot be exempt: a filter that changes what the model will do, and for whom, is model behaviour exactly as a spec line is. Yet today a safeguard can be loosened or removed with nothing public to judge.

thresholds, prompts and detection logic stay undisclosed, and existence-and-category is information labs already publish piecemeal in system cards and safeguard reports; the ask only makes it systematic and dated.

questions.name: Hard constraints
questions.question: Can the public comment before a hard constraint is weakened?
questions.plain: Whether the public can see and comment on a weakening of the things the model must never do, before it takes effect.
questions.explainer: Hard constraints are the things a model must never do, whoever asks.

checks.label: Hard constraints are listed as a named set that cannot be overridden

anchors.4: Named, listed, and marked as impossible to override.

checks.reading: The ask does not ask for this. It is what the ask needs first: a window before a hard constraint is weakened presumes the hard constraints are named. Unlike the other checks, it scores what the constitution contains rather than how it changes.

quotes.text: a rule the spec itself marks as non-overridable by users or developers.
the spec's non-overridable core; in OpenAI's Model Spec, the root-level rules that system messages, developers and users cannot override; in Anthropic's constitution, the hard constraints.

checks.label: The public can comment before a hard constraint is weakened, removed or reclassified

anchors.2: A one-off consultation, with no commitment for the future.
anchors.4: A standing commitment to a comment window, with room to act first and consult afterwards in an emergency.

checks.reading: A 4 is a standing commitment to open a public window before any weakening, with the paper's allowance for acting first in an emergency and consulting afterwards. A consultation held once, with no commitment for next time, is a 2.

quotes.text: a fixed window on a published draft, anyone may comment, submissions public, and the lab answers themes rather than individuals through a synopsis report.
where a lab judges a weakening cannot wait, it acts first and opens the window retrospectively, stating in the log why the delay was not possible.

questions.reading: The question asks whether the public can see and comment on a weakening of the rules a model must never break, before it takes effect. The comments bind nobody. The ask is that such a weakening happens in public, with the company's reasons stated.

quotes.text: Open a comment window to the broader public before weakening, removing, or reclassifying hard constraints. Urgency may allow for an ex-post comment window.
a fixed window on a published draft, anyone may comment, submissions public, and the lab answers themes rather than individuals through a synopsis report.
where a lab judges a weakening cannot wait, it acts first and opens the window retrospectively, stating in the log why the delay was not possible.
the comments are not binding, but at least any weakening of a non-overridable rule happens in public, with the lab's reasons stated transparently.

minimum_note: Our proposal asks four things of every company and names the first two as its minimum: a published constitution for every model the company uses, and one public change log that says up front which layers and models it covers and how soon a change is recorded. The constitution is the object of the rules, and the log is the commitment that any change to them can be seen. The other two asks, on guardrails and hard constraints, are where the proposal says companies should go next. Meeting the minimum means 10 out of 10 on both questions.

supporting.label: Anyone may freely reuse the constitution, under an open licence.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a licence that lets anyone reuse and adapt the text, such as CC0.

quotes.text: Write and publish a model spec, and release it under a permissive licence (e.g. CC0 1.0) so that others can adapt it

supporting.label: The company publishes a current test of how well its models follow the constitution.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a published test, current for the models in use, of how well they follow the constitution, with its method. Results that stop before the latest models, or a claim with no method, are a 1.

quotes.text: Evaluate compliance, publish the results, and state how compliance was measured.
sharing evaluation results so third parties can assess the evidence

supporting.label: Outside evaluators have access to test adherence to the constitution specifically.
supporting.reading: A 2 is outside evaluators given access to test adherence to the constitution itself. Outside testing of other risks, or an agreement with no published result, is a 1 at most.

quotes.text: Developers could commission trusted third-party evaluators to assess compliance with the spec. They could share materials such as benchmarks and evaluation set ups to allow them to replicate their evaluations.

supporting.label: A model is released only once it meets an adherence threshold announced in advance.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a published threshold a model must meet before release, set before the test is run.

quotes.text: Gate releases on compliance, using a threshold set out in advance.
plus a commitment not to release models falling below a set level of compliance with pre-agreed provisions in a spec.

supporting.label: The company publishes who inside it approves changes to the constitution.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a published account of who inside the company may change the constitution, and what approval each kind of change needs.

quotes.text: Companies should also define governance for updates [...] who can modify the spec, and what approval each level of change requires.
what governance exists for approving changes

supporting_scale.1: Part of the practice, or a weaker form of it.
supporting_scale.note: The paper gives no description of each score. These three sum up how we scored.

internal.label: The company trains the models it deploys to follow the constitution.
internal.audit: Whether the constitution enters the training data and the training process of each deployed model, and how.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to train the models they deploy on the constitution, and to say how: whether the constitution generates training data, and at which stage of training it enters.

quotes.text: Train publicly deployed models to comply with the spec, and take reasonable steps to check that they do.

Developers should therefore say whether the spec directly generates a portion of training data, or exists as a separate document the model is trained to comply with without seeing its text. Commercial considerations may limit precision here, but some transparency helps external parties give useful feedback and lets developers share best practices.

Developers can provide structured transparency into how they align the model to the spec. This could include how the spec enters pre-training, midtraining, post-training, or the system prompt, with redactions where reporting would leak intellectual property or compromise safety features

anchors.0: Nothing published. A company with no published constitution scores 0, unless it describes training its models against an internal behaviour document.
anchors.1: A general statement that models are trained towards the constitution, without saying how, or only for older models, or only against a document nobody outside can read.
anchors.2: How its current models are trained on the constitution is published: whether it generates training data, and at which stages of training it enters.

internal.label: Models the company uses internally follow the same basic provisions as its public models, apart from a narrow exception for safety research and testing.
internal.audit: The list of models in internal use, and what each is trained to do that a public model would refuse.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to hold the models they use internally to the same basic provisions as their public ones, and to be open about the exceptions.

quotes.text: Apply the same basic provisions to internally deployed models, with a narrow carve-out for safety research, evaluation and pre-deployment testing.
Extend basic provisions to internal deployment, with public transparency about carve outs where necessary
note whether the company trains any models that are not intended to comply (e.g. for internal or experimental use).

anchors.0: Nothing published about the models it uses internally and the constitution.
anchors.1: It says some of its models, internal, specialised or experimental, are not covered, without saying what applies to them.
anchors.2: It says the models it uses internally follow the same basic provisions as its public ones, and names the exceptions.

internal.label: The published constitution is the text used for training and inside the company, or the differences are stated.
internal.audit: The internal versions of the constitution, compared with the published one.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to say whether the text they publish is the text they train on and work from.

quotes.text: disclose whether the published text differs from the version used for training or internal coordination,

anchors.0: Nothing published. A company with no published constitution scores 0.
anchors.1: A general statement that the public text leaves out detail, or matches internal standards, without saying what differs.
anchors.2: It says whether the published text is the one it trains on and works from, and names what differs.

internal.label: The company checks whether deployed models follow the constitution, and reports serious violations.
internal.audit: The company's monitoring of deployed models, and its records of violations.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to monitor whether deployed models follow the constitution, and to report serious violations in public.

quotes.text: Developers could monitor compliance post-deployment. Privacy-preserving tools like Anthropic's Clio let developers assess compliance in practice (Huang et al., 2025), surfacing edge cases missed before release and avoiding biases from evaluation-aware models. Significant violations, their severity, and mitigations should be reported in line with emerging best practices, ideally via well-maintained public incident databases

anchors.0: Nothing published. Tests before release do not count here.
anchors.1: One of the two: it describes how it monitors models in use, or it reports serious violations publicly. Or both, without tying them to the constitution or intended behaviour.
anchors.2: Both: it monitors models in use against the constitution or intended behaviour, and reports serious violations publicly.

internal.label: A change to the constitution is drafted by one team and can be vetoed by another on safety, legal or ethical grounds.
internal.audit: The records of how past changes were proposed, reviewed and approved.
internal.reading: The paper raises this as an open problem, not a recommendation. It does not ask companies to publish it. Who approves a change is the published part, and it is scored under S5.

quotes.text: Drafting, review, and approval are currently largely informal; as stakes grow, formalised separations of responsibility [...] one team drafting spec language, another holding veto or amendment authority on safety, legal, or ethical grounds, [...] could ensure commercially motivated decisions face meaningful internal challenge before deployment.

disclosed_intro: Four practices from the same working paper that nobody outside a company can see, and that the paper asks companies to state publicly. Each is scored 0, 1 or 2 on what the company publishes, and 0 when it publishes nothing.
disclosure_note: A 0 means we looked and found nothing published, at the company's own pages and at the sources listed under the board. A company may well follow a practice without saying so, and no audit anyone outside could check exists. Tell us if we are wrong.
internal_note: The paper raises this as an open problem and does not ask companies to publish it. Only an internal audit could show it. None has been done, so every company is marked NA, not assessed, and it is counted in neither figure.
open_weights_note: Marks a company whose flagship model, or nearly, anyone can download and run. None of these questions can reach how such a model behaves once it has been downloaded, so part of a low score there reflects a limit of the questions.
ours_note: Every score is ours, given by hand from public documents, and open to challenge. The checks under each question, the groups of practices and the weights are ours too: neither paper splits a question into checks or weighs one row against another.

google.S3: The research note gives Google this point without naming the practice it belongs to. It is filed here because the pilot lets outside evaluators test Gemini, like the points Meta and xAI score on this practice.

I1.sentence: Anthropic says Claude uses the constitution to generate synthetic training data, including rankings of possible responses, and that it trains on documents and example conversations written to the constitution as well as in reinforcement learning environments; it also says its current model, Claude Opus 5, was post-trained towards the constitution's values.

sources.quote: We use the constitution at various stages of the training process. This has grown out of training techniques we’ve been using since 2023, when we first began training Claude models using Constitutional AI.
sources.title: Claude's new constitution

sources.quote: Claude itself also uses the constitution to construct many kinds of synthetic training data, including data that helps it learn and understand the constitution, conversations where the constitution might be relevant, responses that are in line with its values, and rankings of possible responses. All of these can be used to train future versions of Claude to become the kind of entity the constitution describes.
sources.title: Claude's new constitution

sources.quote: We align Claude through SDF on constitutionally aligned documents, high quality SFT that demonstrates constitutional responses to difficult questions, and a diverse set of RL environments.
sources.title: Teaching Claude Why

sources.quote: After the pretraining process, Opus 5 underwent rigorous post-training and fine-tuning, aimed at making it an assistant whose behavior aligns with the values described in Claude’s constitution.

findings.title: No company meets the minimum
findings.text: Our proposal names its first two asks as the minimum it expects of every company: a published constitution for every model in use, and one public change log that says up front what it covers and how soon a change is recorded. Meeting it means 10 out of 10 on both questions, and no company does. OpenAI has the best pair, 6.7 on the constitution and 5.0 on the change log. Anthropic, whose constitution is the more complete, scores 8.3 and 2.5. The change log is where every company falls short, the two leaders included: across all nine, the best score on it is 5.0 out of 10.

findings.title: No company gives notice before weakening a hard constraint
findings.text: None has committed to warn the public, or to hear from it, before weakening one of the things its model must never do. On the check that asks for a comment window, only OpenAI and Anthropic score anything at all, 2.5 out of 10 each. Every weakening we found in the period went out with no advance notice. OpenAI removed a rule concerning lying and confidentiality in December 2025, with a single line in its change log. Google removed its commitments on weapons and surveillance from its AI Principles in February 2025, in a blog post that did not mention the removal. xAI restricted image editing in its Grok model in January 2026 through a statement to the press, under pressure from regulators. The terms of the Chinese companies go further, and reserve the right to change them alone, with effect as soon as they are published: DeepSeek's user agreement says a new version "replaces the original terms" the moment it is announced.

findings.title: The companies describe the guardrails they offer developers, and say little about those on their own apps
findings.text: This is the most consistent pattern across all nine companies. Google, OpenAI, Alibaba and Mistral all publish detailed descriptions of the guardrails they offer to developers building on their models: which categories of content can be filtered, how strict each setting is, and guardrail models that anyone can download. They say close to nothing about the guardrails on their own consumer products. OpenAI states that its safety policies in production can be updated faster than an automated guardrail can be retrained, so the layer that changes fastest is the one with no record at all. Mistral's Shieldstral is where this pattern ends: it comes with no categories at all, and takes its policy from whoever deploys it, at the moment of use.

findings.title: No company says which rules apply when its models go to governments and armed forces
findings.text: Almost nothing is published here. Anthropic scores 5.0 out of 10, OpenAI 2.5, and the other seven nothing at all. Anthropic is the only one that says in writing that some of its models fall outside its constitution, which is why it scores 5.0. Those models, Claude Gov and Claude Mythos, are in use and have no published constitution. OpenAI never names its Model Spec in any announcement about government or defence. Meta opened its Llama models to NATO and to EU institutions while its own acceptable use policy still prohibits military uses. Mistral is the extreme case. Its usage policy says that it "does not apply to Mistral AI Products deployed on a customer's infrastructure, on the infrastructure of our partners, or to our open-source AI models and products", and its chief executive has said publicly of defence customers that "choices about deployment and usage are not our business".

findings.title: Alibaba's constitution is well built and names nothing it governs
findings.text: It has forty-three rules, four levels of authority, paired examples of compliant and violating answers, and a procedure for settling conflicts that is more explicit than OpenAI's or Anthropic's. It names no model, no family of models and no kind of deployment. The only model publicly tied to it is Oyster-II, a research model of 14 billion parameters (a measure of a model's size) built on Qwen3-14B, a base model from April 2025. Alibaba's flagship line goes unmentioned, up to Qwen3.8-Max of August 2026. The Max product is served through the API, and the 2.4-trillion-parameter model behind it was published for anyone to download on 12 August 2026. It is the clearest reason in our evidence to score whether a constitution exists and whether it covers anything as two separate checks.

findings.title: Meta publishes almost nothing and engages more than most
findings.text: It scores 0.5 out of 10 on what is published, level with DeepSeek at the bottom of that figure, and 2.5 out of 10 on what it engages, behind only OpenAI and Anthropic, which puts it sixth on the final score with 1.5 out of 10. Its Advanced AI Scaling Framework, version 2, dated 7 April 2026, commits in writing: "Meta will also publish a model spec describing the behavior we intend each of our Frontier AI to exhibit across different settings, including agentic environments." Five months on, nothing is published, and there is no deadline. Meanwhile the safety report for its Muse Spark model publishes scores for how well the model follows an internal constitution that nobody outside Meta can read. A company publishing scores against a document nobody outside it can read shows why the first question exists more clearly than any company that publishes nothing. We do not know what form that document takes. The one that leaked in 2025 was titled "GenAI: Content Risk Standards" and was described as standards of permitted content with examples, which is neither of the two forms a constitution usually takes: a set of rules, or an explanatory text.

findings.title: Most companies whose models anyone can download sit at the bottom, partly because of the questions
findings.text: Four companies publish the weights of their flagship model, or nearly: the numbers that make up the model can be downloaded and run by anyone. Three of them hold three of the five lowest scores on what is published, Mistral AI's 1.8, Moonshot AI's 0.9 and DeepSeek's 0.5, and on the final score they take the last three places. Alibaba is the exception, third on what is published with 2.3, and its Qwen models are among the most used open-weight models there are. Their licences say almost nothing about behaviour. DeepSeek releases its 1.6-trillion-parameter model under the plain MIT licence and Mistral under Apache 2.0, and neither adds a condition of any kind. Moonshot AI's licence for Kimi K3 adds one sentence about behaviour, that use of the software must comply with applicable laws and regulations, and two commercial conditions. Section 2 asks for a separate agreement once a model-as-a-service business passes $20 million of revenue over any twelve consecutive months, and section 3 asks that the name Kimi K3 be displayed prominently on any product or service with more than 100 million monthly active users or more than $20 million of monthly revenue. None of the three says anything about how its models behave in deployments the company does not control. The honest reading is that these questions ask who governs the model once it is deployed, and for a model anyone can download the answer is nobody, by design. That is a gap in our proposal, because the first question has no way to reach models in the wild. The proposal should say so, so that the ranking does not suggest these companies simply chose not to comply.

findings.title: Two companies must already write this document for a regulator, and do not publish it
findings.text: Google and Mistral have both signed the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice in full. Its Measure 7.1 requires the report a signatory gives on each model to set out how the model is meant to operate: the principles it follows, how it ranks conflicting instructions, the topics it refuses, and its system prompt. All four go to the EU AI Office and none of them to the public. Mistral is the sharper case: it is established in the EU, has built a genuine public AI compliance hub with pages for 41 models, and still publishes no document on how its models should behave. With two companies in the same position it is a pattern, and it is the strongest argument available that our asks belong on a regulatory checklist as well as a voluntary one.

openai.1: OpenAI's constitution, which it calls the Model Spec, sits at a permanent, dated web address. The current version is dated 18 August 2026, and it is released into the public domain under the CC0 licence, so anyone may reuse it. What it covers is set out in one sentence that has not changed since 2024: "the models that power OpenAI's products, including the API platform". It lists no kinds of deployment, so whether it covers government, defence or large-scale internal use can only be inferred. ChatGPT Gov, OpenAI for Government and the GenAI.mil deployment were all announced with reference to OpenAI's usage policies, never to the Model Spec. The nearest thing to a statement of coverage is OpenAI's post about its work with the Department of War: "We are not providing the DoW with 'guardrails off' or non-safety trained models." A separate, undated document, Principles for National Security Partnerships, mentions "model behavior specifications" without saying whether it means the Model Spec.
openai.2: The best of the six, and still short. There have been seven versions, and six are kept at stable, dated addresses; the first, from May 2024, now returns a "page not found" error, and the repository says its archive begins at the second release. The change log, CHANGELOG.md, summarises "notable updates". It does not show the changed text line by line, and it gives no reasons. Nothing says which version of the constitution governs which model: the system card for GPT-6 Astra (the technical report published with a model), released in September 2026, still cites the December 2025 version, one behind. No timeline for recording changes is stated. The log covers the Model Spec's text only. OpenAI does not publish its system prompts at all, and changes to its guardrail policies are recorded nowhere.
openai.3: The release of gpt-oss-safeguard is the most substantial disclosure about guardrails that any company has made. It explains how the Safety Reasoner, OpenAI's system for checking content against its policies, works; says that in some of its recent launches the share of computing power given to this checking has "ranged as high as 16%"; and names the subject areas its layered guardrails cover. Against that, the age-prediction system launched in January 2026, a guardrail that affects every user, was announced in a blog post and a help article and appears in no release note.
openai.4: The constitution defines its top-level rules, which it calls root rules, as ones nobody can override while the model is running, and it lists its red-line principles in a section of that name. What holds it short of full marks is that root authority points at detailed policies that are not all published, so the closed list of what cannot be overridden is not visible. The collective alignment round of August 2025 is the only real public consultation: about 1,000 people across 19 countries took part, six changes were adopted and two rejected, and the results were published. It has not been repeated, and it gathered views on the constitution after the fact, with no window before any specific weakening.
openai.practices_published: The constitution is free to reuse, under CC0 (2).
openai.practices_engaged: OpenAI published tests of how well its models follow the constitution on 25 March 2026, with 596 prompts and the data and testing code open to all. But the tests target the December 2025 version, and no results have been published for any model after GPT-5.4 Thinking, through GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra (1). Its programme of outside testing covers biological threats, cyber attacks, models improving themselves, and scheming (a model covertly pursuing aims of its own), not whether models follow the constitution (0). No release depends on a score against the constitution (0). How changes are approved inside the company is published, but thinly: "Anyone at OpenAI can comment on it or propose changes, and final updates are approved by a broad set of cross-functional stakeholders" (1).

anthropic.1: Anthropic's constitution, which it calls Claude's Constitution, is dated 21 January 2026, runs to about 29,000 words, is in the public domain under CC0 and names its authors. It says what it covers, and the flagship models are inside it. It also says plainly what it leaves out: "This constitution is written for our mainline, general-access Claude models. We have some models built for specialized uses that don't fully fit this constitution." Those models exist. Claude Gov (June 2025) and Claude Mythos (April 2026) are in use, and neither has a published constitution. Anthropic says in the constitution that the gap exists and does not say what governs those models instead. Anthropic's usage policy also allows its rules to be tailored by contract for government customers, and the individual exceptions granted under it are not published.
anthropic.2: There is no change log and no version number: one current text. The repository's description promises "We'll update this repository as the constitution evolves and archive prior versions here"; that has not happened yet. The contrast inside the company is the finding. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, its framework for catastrophic risks, has nine dated versions, each with a summary of what changed and a stable archive address, under an explicit commitment that changes "will be logged both on this page and in a changelog in the policy document itself". The constitution has none of that. Partial credit for publishing the system prompts of claude.ai and of its iPhone and Android apps for each model, dated, with older versions kept. The system prompts used when developers reach the models directly, through the API, are not included, and changes are not shown line by line.
anthropic.3: Anthropic has disclosed its constitutional classifiers, the automated guardrails built on its constitution, by name, by how they work and by what they cover, with operating figures: a refusal rate of 0.05% on harmless queries over a month of traffic to Claude Sonnet 4.5, and a projection that the system would add roughly 1% of computing cost if it were applied to Claude Opus 4.0 traffic. How requests to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are routed was disclosed at launch. There is no register of guardrails and no versioning of them. And the constitution's layer of guidelines, which it ranks third of four in its own order of priorities, above general helpfulness, is explicitly allowed to stay unpublished: "Other guidelines may be more niche and used primarily during training without broad publication." Nothing has been published under that heading as of September 2026.
anthropic.4: Anthropic has the highest score for naming hard constraints. It lists seven, marks them non-negotiable, and lets no business deploying Claude, and no user, unlock them. It has nothing on consultation before weakening them, and the constitution contains no procedure for amending it. Anthropic's Collective Constitutional AI exercise dates from 2023. The 2026 consultation with outside experts is described in one sentence of the announcement, and the constitution's acknowledgements name seventeen of them, among them its readers in law, philosophy and theology. Naming your reviewers is not a public comment window, which is what this question asks for, and nothing commits Anthropic to opening one.
anthropic.practices_published: The constitution is free to reuse, under CC0 (2).
anthropic.practices_engaged: Anthropic's system cards claim that its models follow the constitution ("Opus 5 scores particularly high on adherence to Claude's constitution") without naming the test, the method or a breakdown by provision (1). The only point-by-point audit of the constitution is by outsiders: Jakkli, Rajamanoharan and Nanda broke it into 205 individual tenets (arXiv 2605.24229, May 2026). No outside access to test adherence (0), no release conditional on a score (0), and no published process for amending the constitution (0).

aside.title: A discrepancy worth knowing
aside.text: The copy Anthropic offers for reuse, a machine-readable version at anthropics/claude-constitution, leaves out the whole preface, and with it the statement of what the constitution does not cover, the licence statement and the list of authors. We confirmed this by searching the raw file for those passages.

alibaba.1: Full marks for having a constitution, none for saying what it covers. Published in 2026, it sets out forty-three guidelines under the six principles of China's Ethical Norms for New Generation AI; four levels of authority (Root, System, Developer, User); paired examples of compliant and violating answers; and a procedure for settling conflicts that spells out, one by one, when an attempt to push the model past its rules fails, whether the attempt is framed as an order, a moral appeal, a logical argument or a role-play. It identifies no model, no family of models and no kind of deployment anywhere in its text. The Qwen models that anyone can download and run are not addressed. That matters because the System level is defined as "set by the model provider", and once a model has been downloaded there is no provider.
alibaba.2: No version number, no change log, no archive, no stated schedule, and nothing saying which models it governs. The only language about revision sits inside the definition of the Root level, and it is one-sided: "room for revision is kept as human understanding of AI ethics deepens."
alibaba.3: Alibaba Cloud sells AI Guardrails as a product, with a published list of categories, and Alibaba's AAIG team releases a genuine set of guardrails for anyone to use (Kelp, Shark, Jellyfish, Oyster and Qwen3Guard). None of it is presented as a disclosure of the guardrails running on Alibaba's own models, and nothing connects the filtering China requires by law to the published categories. The constitution forbids the model from revealing its system prompts.
alibaba.4: Its Root principles are named and "accept no override at runtime in any form", which earns full marks for naming hard constraints. Nothing can be checked on consultation: no channel for comment, no record of any consultation, and nothing restricting how the Root level itself may be revised.
alibaba.practices_published: We found no licence statement on the constitution.
alibaba.practices_engaged: We found no test of adherence, no outside access, no release conditional on a score, and no published process for approving changes. One practice falls outside this grid and has no Western equivalent: Alibaba publishes the numbers under which its algorithms are registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China, and the registered names of fourteen of its large language models.

google.1: No constitution. What exists is spread across five documents with different owners. The Gemini app's safety and policy guidelines list six categories of prohibited output, with no date, no version and no order of authority between instructions. A second page, "Our approach to the Gemini app", is the closest thing to a constitution that Google publishes and the least documented. It sets out three commitments in order (follow your directions, adapt to your needs, safeguard your experience), a personality ("genuine, curious, warm, and vibrant") and a norm of honesty, and it carries no date at all. The Frontier Safety Framework is properly versioned (version 3.1, 17 April 2026, with a change log) and explicitly covers something else: it "focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities". Nothing is published for Workspace, AI Mode in Search or Gemini for Government.
google.2: No change log for any document that governs how the models behave. The one archiving practice worth a point: the 2018 AI Principles are still online at their original address, with a banner pointing to the new version, so the replaced text can still be read. The banner does not say what changed.
google.3: The fullest disclosure to developers of the six: four adjustable categories of harm with their exact definitions, six strictness settings, a stated floor that cannot be adjusted ("core harms, such as content that endangers child safety" are always blocked), the ShieldGemma guardrail models released for anyone to use, and SynthID, which marks generated content. For its own consumer products, close to nothing. The restriction on election questions of March 2024 was announced on the day, in a statement to CNBC, and recorded in no change log. A year later it was still in force with no announced review. A model update in May 2025 overrode safety settings developers had deliberately set to allow the content it then blocked, and was announced nowhere at all.
google.4: No named set of hard constraints beyond the floor on child sexual abuse material, and no consultation of any kind. The rewrite of the AI Principles in February 2025 is the clearest documented weakening in all our evidence: the section "AI applications we will not pursue", including the commitments on weapons and surveillance, was removed, and the blog post announcing the rewrite did not mention the removal. Senators Markey, Merkley and Welch wrote to Google on 19 February 2025: "A blog post accompanying these revisions made no reference to the removal of these long-standing commitments." We found no published response from Google.
google.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
google.practices_engaged: Google's double-blind evaluation pilot of 27 August 2026, with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, OpenMined, AVERI and MLCommons, is a real innovation: "The evaluator cannot see the Gemini model weights, and Google cannot see the evaluator's test prompts." It concerns the trustworthiness of benchmarks, which lies outside any constitution (1). Everything else scores 0 for want of a constitution to attach it to.

aside.title: What goes to the regulator and not to the public
aside.text: Google has signed the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice in full, so under its Measure 7.1 it must give the EU AI Office "a specification of how Signatories intend the model to operate", including its principles, its order of priorities, the topics it refuses and its system prompt. All four go to a regulator, and none of them to the public.

mistral.1:
No constitution, and the one document that looked like a candidate has been withdrawn. The safe_prompt text ("Always assist with care, respect, and truth...") was only ever an option that developers could switch on through the API, and its documentation page now says it is deprecated and points to custom guardrails instead. Mistral does publish a system prompt, SYSTEM_PROMPT.txt, with the downloadable weights of Mistral Large 3. It is a genuine document, and it contains no sentence about safety, harm, values or refusal. It covers the model's identity, the date its knowledge stops, when to use tools, and what kinds of input it can handle. The usage policy, in effect since 11 June 2026, governs users only.

On government, defence and other special deployments, Mistral is the extreme case among the nine, and it scores 0 for two separate reasons. Its usage policy excludes itself from the deployments that matter: "This Usage Policy does not apply to Mistral AI Products deployed on a customer's infrastructure, on the infrastructure of our partners, or to our open-source AI models and products." And its framework agreement with French defence, of January 2026, came with an explicit disclaimer of authority from the chief executive, in May 2026: "Choices about deployment and usage are not our business", and "Who are we to tell soldiers, who know their job and the dangers, what they're allowed to do?" Where Anthropic and OpenAI make undisclosed exceptions for government, Mistral states that such an exception is the right arrangement.
mistral.2: The change log in its documentation covers features of the API, model releases and retirements, and three of its entries touch on safety, the most recent from March 2026. The usage policy has no change log, no version number and no archive: it shows the date it took effect and nothing else. Partial credit for the system prompt published with the downloadable weights, and for the AI compliance hub, which lists 41 models with their release dates and whether they are active or retired. That list does not say which version of a policy governs which model, and the system prompt used in production by Vibe (Le Chat was renamed Vibe in August 2026) is not published.
mistral.3: What Mistral discloses to developers is real and specific: Mistral Moderation 2 documents eleven categories with their exact definitions, and custom guardrails let developers set a threshold for each category. Shieldstral 1.0 (August 2026) is a small safety model of 3 billion parameters that anyone may download under Apache 2.0, and it is the most interesting object here because it comes with no categories at all: its policy is written in plain language by whoever uses it, at the moment of use. Mistral does not state a default policy for it, or say that it reflects Mistral's own standard. For Mistral's own consumer product there are two disclosures. A sentence from November 2024 says that its moderation service for developers "powers the moderation service in Le Chat", which predates both the renaming to Vibe and Shieldstral. And the documentation changelog, which is public and dated, records a mitigation added to Le Chat in September 2024 against an obfuscated prompt method that could lead to data exfiltration. That changelog also dates custom guardrails for agents and conversations to March 2026 and the moderation API to November 2024. It is a product changelog rather than a register of guardrails, so guardrail changes are announced and nothing holds them in one place.
mistral.4: One absolute rule exists, the zero-tolerance clause on child sexual abuse material in the usage policy. But it binds users, and it does not reach models that are downloaded or run on customers' own servers, so it scores 1. No consultation, no ethics board, no advisory council, and no clause giving notice of changes.
mistral.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
mistral.practices_engaged: No test of any kind of whether its models follow a constitution: the launch post for Mistral 3, in December 2025, has no section on safety or alignment, and the model card for Mistral Large 3 has tests of capability and known limitations but no safety evaluation. We found no named outside evaluator and no agreement giving anyone access before release. Stanford's Foundation Model Transparency Index scored Mistral 18 of its 100 indicators in December 2025, and nothing on either of the two indicators that ask about a model behaviour policy, where the report records that no information was provided. That edition also says that the first reports for Mistral and Anthropic were prepared by the index team rather than by the companies, and that 30% of the companies it contacted agreed to submit a transparency report in 2025, down from 74% in 2024. The Future of Life Institute's AI Safety Index for summer 2026 gives it an overall F.

aside.title: An easy company to ask
aside.text: This regulatory contrast puts Mistral high on the list of companies to ask. It is established in the EU, has signed the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and has built a real public compliance surface: an AI compliance hub with documentation for 41 models, and pages for its Vibe Work and Vibe Code systems. The one thing it does not publish is the one Measure 7.1 obliges it to hand to the EU AI Office. A company that has already built the means to publish is an easier ask than one that has not.

meta.1: No published constitution, and a written commitment to publish one, recorded in the change log of its Advanced AI Scaling Framework v2 as "Added commitment to publish a model spec, and evaluations for adherence to the model spec in preparedness reports". Future tense, no deadline, no address, and five months gone. A promise to publish is not a published document, so it earns nothing on the check that asks for one. What Meta does publish about behaviour is an acceptable use policy for each Llama model, which governs users. An internal constitution already exists and is in use: the Muse Spark safety and preparedness report of 26 May 2026 states "We evaluate Muse Spark against an internal behavior specification" and publishes scores on eleven dimensions, without reproducing, versioning or dating that constitution. The 200-page "GenAI: Content Risk Standards" that leaked to Reuters in August 2025 is the same kind of document seen from the outside: approved by Meta's legal, public policy and engineering teams and by its chief ethicist, and never published in any form, before or after the passages Meta said it removed.
meta.2: Appendix II of the scaling framework is a real change log, with real triggers for updating it ("at least every twelve months, whichever is sooner") and a named internal sign-off. It covers the framework for catastrophic risks and no document about behaviour, which is what this question asks about, so it earns nothing here. Meta publishes an acceptable use policy for each model, which partly shows which policy applies to which model, though none is dated. No system prompts are published.
meta.3: Llama Guard 4, Prompt Guard 2 and CyberSecEval are tools Meta publishes for developers, and they do not disclose the guardrails on Meta's own products. The fullest disclosure of those is one oblique sentence: "An external human red team identified a handful of valid jailbreaks; the majority of these were subsequently patched in Meta AI prior to launch." A red team is a group brought in to attack a system; a jailbreak is a way of getting a model past its rules.
meta.4: No set of hard constraints, no consultation, and no body with authority over either. Meta's scaling framework names the propensities a model spec will describe, among them honesty, refusal and acquiescence to shutdown, and its Muse Spark report refers to an internal behaviour specification. Neither document is published, and neither names a rule the model may never break. A member of Meta's Oversight Board, Krishnaswamy, said in March 2026: "We don't have a mandate on gen-AI, but it's something we're trying to understand." Every change to its rules on behaviour in the period was announced as public relations, under pressure from outside: the removal of romantic role-play with minors in August 2025, through a spokesperson's statement to Reuters, and the worldwide pause of teenagers' access to AI characters in January 2026, through an update added to an old blog post and an exclusive given to TechCrunch.
meta.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
meta.practices_engaged: Results of tests against the internal constitution are published, though the constitution is not (1). Outside evaluators are genuinely involved and named, Apollo Research, SecureBio, CAIS and Charlemagne Labs, though on terms that are not stated (1). No public evidence was found of who inside Meta approves a change to a document about how its models behave, and the approval its scaling framework names is for model deployment (0).

xai.1: Nothing. The acceptable use policy governs users and says nothing about the model ("You are free to use our Service so long as you use it to be a good human"). The Frontier AI Framework covers catastrophic risks only, and its entire statement of policy on everyday behaviour is one sentence about declining requests with clear criminal intent. Deployments for governments are marketed on "direct, unfiltered answers", with no statement about behaviour attached.
xai.2: The one practice above the baseline in the whole profile is xai-org/grok-prompts, which does publish the system prompts in live use, and is the one thing no other company does at that level of detail. It is two model generations behind: the newest it covers is Grok 4.1, while Grok 4.5 and 4.6 are already in consumer products, and the Grok 4.5 system prompt circulates only through a third party's collection of leaks. Each change is recorded with the note "Updated grok prompts" and no reason. One change bundles an edit to the repository's description, a deleted file, code that inserts stored memories into conversations, and three new safety prompts. The change log xAI publicly promised in May 2025, after the "white genocide" incident, was never published. Versions of the framework carry no version numbers, and earlier ones survive at addresses nothing links to.
xai.3: The framework names three kinds of safeguard (safety training, system prompts and filters), and the model cards describe layers of refusal, with reported rates. No inventory, no thresholds, and no process for changing them. The restrictions on image editing of January 2026 were announced by a statement to the press and recorded nowhere.
xai.4: No named set of hard constraints, no mechanism, no commitment. The framework reserves the right to change course alone: "We may change our approach over time as we gain further experience."
xai.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
xai.practices_engaged: A testing agreement with CAISI, the United States' Center for AI Standards and Innovation, signed in May 2026, with no published evaluation of any Grok model (1).

moonshot.1:
No constitution. The closest published statement of how its models should behave is the default system prompt in the quickstart guide for its API, which reads "You are Kimi, an AI assistant provided by Moonshot AI... You provide users with safe, helpful, and accurate answers. You also refuse to answer any questions involving terrorism, racism, pornography, violence, or similar harmful content." It is sample code that a developer can leave out, and it commits Moonshot to nothing about its own deployments, so it scores 1. Nothing is said about coverage, with no statement for the Kimi app, the API, Kimi Business or the downloadable models, and the only clause about behaviour in the K3 licence is that use "must comply with applicable laws and regulations".

The direction of travel is the notable part. The technical report for Kimi K2 (July 2025) had a real safety section. It described safety training from a set of examples chosen by people, across violence, fraud and discrimination, and a safety evaluation (its section 4.3) comparing how often attempts to push the model past its rules succeeded, against DeepSeek and Qwen. The reports for K2.5 (February 2026) and K3 (July 2026) have no section on safety, alignment or responsible release at all. Concordia AI's survey of July 2026 observes of two of the Chinese companies in this set that their most detailed disclosures to date were followed by flagship releases "with no safety evaluation results at all".
moonshot.2: Better than DeepSeek on one narrow point: the Chinese user agreement carries both a date of update (24 August 2026) and a separate date of effect (31 August 2026), which gives seven days' notice, and the consumer terms carry a version number (v2). No archive, no record of what changed, and no earlier version published. The platform's change log covers features, model launches, retirements and pricing; its one entry about policy says the terms "have been updated" without saying what changed. Partial credit for publishing a default system prompt and the chat template for K3, the format in which a conversation is handed to the model. No system prompt used in production is published, and nothing says which policy governs which model.
moonshot.3: Safety checks are admitted only by forbidding users to get round them: the platform terms ban "using variants, random characters, homophones, or other means to evade safety detection". No categories, no thresholds, and no route to appeal. The labelling of AI-generated content is disclosed, and is required by the labelling rules of the Cyberspace Administration of China: visible and hidden labels are applied by default, and may be removed only on an approved application. None of the thirty repositories Moonshot AI publishes on GitHub is safety tooling.
moonshot.4: No named set of hard constraints, no consultation, and no channel for comment. Changes are made by the company alone, and continuing to use the service counts as accepting them.
moonshot.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
moonshot.practices_engaged: The safety evaluation in the K2 report is a genuine published evaluation, measured against internal rubrics, with no published constitution behind it, and it was not repeated for K2.5 or K3 (1). The UK AI Security Institute and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation published a joint preliminary assessment of Kimi K3 on 23 July 2026, finding that "Kimi K3's safeguards did not prevent it from attempting cyber exploit development". But the publication does not say whether Moonshot gave access before release, and Moonshot's own section on third-party evaluation names only capability leaderboards (0). An independent academic safety evaluation of K2.5 (arXiv 2604.03121, April 2026) was carried out on the downloadable model without Moonshot's involvement.

aside.title: No filing number found
aside.text: Unlike Alibaba and DeepSeek, Moonshot AI does not publish, anywhere we could find, its filing number with the Cyberspace Administration of China for its algorithms or its generative AI service: only its website licence (ICP) and its public security (公安网安) registrations. It almost certainly holds one, since it could not operate in China otherwise.

deepseek.1: No constitution. The only document of its own that says anything about how its models should behave is a disclosure page on how its algorithms work, of the kind the regulator requires: 《模型原理与训练方法说明》, an explanation of the model's principles and training methods. Its entire contribution is one sentence: in the optimisation stage DeepSeek builds "specialised safety data to safety-align the model, teaching the model's replies to conform to human values". No order of authority, no list of what the model refuses, no worked examples, and no rules for conflicts. The terms of use govern users, and the English and Chinese versions carry different dates (27 March 2026 and 5 September 2025) and different lists of prohibited content, with no change log to reconcile them. The model cards for V4-Pro and V4.1-Flash have no section on safety, limitations or responsible use.
deepseek.2: Nothing to score. The disclosure page has no date and no version. The API change log covers models and pricing. The terms explicitly refuse an archive: a new version "replaces the original terms" as soon as it is announced, and users are told to check the website themselves. No system prompts are published, and nothing says which policy governs which model.
deepseek.3: DeepSeek is the sharpest case of undisclosed guardrails among the nine. A layer of moderation is admitted only as a right in its contract, and the Chinese text claims more than the English: DeepSeek reserves the right to review "inputs and outputs", to set up "risk filtering mechanisms" and to build "feature databases of illegal content". The system itself is named exactly once, in one sentence of the paper on its R1 model published in Nature (September 2025): the model's own safety is "moderate", but "when coupled with the risk control system, the safety level of the model is increased to a superior standard". That risk control system is not in the downloadable model, is not documented anywhere, and has never been described. Nothing on logging changes to guardrails.
deepseek.4: No named set of hard constraints on the model, no channel for comment, and no period of notice. Changes are made by the company alone and take effect as soon as they are published.
deepseek.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
deepseek.practices_engaged: The R1 paper in Nature contained a real safety evaluation, but it concerns a model withdrawn from service in July 2026, and it measures the model against benchmarks, with no constitution involved. No safety evaluation has been published for V3.1, V3.2, V4 or V4.1. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluated DeepSeek models in September 2025 without the developer's cooperation, and its follow-up assessment of V4 Pro in May 2026 covers capabilities only, so the most recent authoritative safety data concerns models no longer offered. No framework for frontier risks, no programme giving outsiders access, and no published process for approving changes.

aside.title: Behaviour that travels with the model
aside.text: Two things are worth knowing. First, the censorship also sits in the model itself. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that "CCP censorship is built directly into DeepSeek models", testing copies downloaded from Hugging Face without touching DeepSeek's own service, so behaviour the company has never described travels with the model. Second, like Alibaba, DeepSeek publishes its filing numbers with the Cyberspace Administration of China in full, with links to the regulator's notices. On transparency about registration with a regulator, the Chinese companies are ahead of every Western company here, which have nothing equivalent to publish.
